Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

derivations.claim: With the stated orientation, the four boundary contributions are $\int_{y_0}^{y_1}E_y(x_0,y,z_0)\,dy$, $\int_{z_0}^{z_1}E_z(x_0,y_1,z)\,dz$, $-\int_{y_0}^{y_1}E_y(x_0,y,z_1)\,dy$, and $-\int_{z_0}^{z_1}E_z(x_0,y_0,z)\,dz$. Apply [F1] to the two differences to rewrite their sum as $-\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\int_{z_0}^{z_1}\partial_zE_y\,dz\,dy+\int_{z_0}^{z_1}\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\partial_yE_z\,dy\,dz$.

The two integrands $\partial_yE_z$ and $\partial_zE_y$ are continuous on the compact rectangle, so each is Riemann integrable by [F2]. Riemann–Fubini [F3] identifies each double integral with either order of its iterated integral. Thus the $\partial_yE_z$ term in step 1.1 can be written in the same $dy$-then-$dz$ order as the other term.

Combining the two terms from step 1.1 using the ordering justified in step 2.1 gives $\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\int_{z_0}^{z_1}(\partial_yE_z-\partial_zE_y)\,dz\,dy$, exactly the $x$-component of the curl flux. Cyclic relabeling gives the other coordinate faces; reversing the orientation changes the sign of every boundary and flux term.

Let $K$ be a finite oriented three-dimensional cell complex with vertex, edge, face, and volume cochains. An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. Write $N_v,N_e,N_f,N_c$ for the retained vertex, edge, face, and cell counts. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

The electric, magnetic, and conductive material matrices are real symmetric matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, $M_b\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_f}$, and $S\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, respectively. The first two are positive definite and represent the discrete weighted inner products induced by $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$; $S$ is positive semidefinite and represents conductivity. Write $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle_{M_e}=e_1^TM_ee_2$, $\langle b_1,b_2\rangle_{M_b}=b_1^TM_bb_2$, and $\|e\|_{M_e}^2=\langle e,e\rangle_{M_e}$, $\|b\|_{M_b}^2=\langle b,b\rangle_{M_b}$. In a homogeneous isotropic periodic Cartesian grid with spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$ and cell volume $V=h_xh_yh_z$, the diagonal entries for an $x$-edge and an $x$-normal face are $\epsilon V/h_x^2=\epsilon h_yh_z/h_x$ and $\mu^{-1}h_x/(h_yh_z)$; the $y$ and $z$ entries are obtained by cyclic permutation. These values are dual-volume Hodge weights for line-integral and face-flux cochains. A compatible PEC closure uses the corresponding truncated dual volumes for free electric edges, while the magnetic mass includes boundary faces; the resulting matrices remain positive definite. The discrete constraints are $G^TM_ee^n=\rho^n$ on interior vertices and $Db^{n-1/2}=0$ on all cells.

For current cochains $j^{n+1/2}$ and charge rows $\rho^n$, the discrete continuity condition means
$$\rho^{n+1}-\rho^n+\Delta t\,G^T\left(j^{n+1/2}+S\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)=0.$$
For PEC this is the interior-vertex volume-charge relation; this closure has no separate boundary surface-charge/current cochain.

The cochain identities $CG=0$ and $DC=0$ are not imposed as an extra numerical approximation: they follow from oriented boundary-of-boundary cancellation, including the PEC row and column restrictions, as proved in [[lem-maxwell-discrete-incidence-identities]]. No cell geometry picture is used as a proof.

derivations.claim: On an oriented triangle with ordered vertices $[v_0,v_1,v_2]$, the coboundary of a vertex cochain $q$ evaluated on the triangle is its oriented edge sum $(q(v_1)-q(v_0))+(q(v_2)-q(v_1))+(q(v_0)-q(v_2))=0$. Hence each triangular face row of $CG$ vanishes. The same calculation is the transpose of $partial_1\partial_2=0$ under the incidence convention in [F1].

On an oriented tetrahedron, each edge in the boundary of its oriented boundary is obtained by deleting two different vertices. For each such pair of deleted indices, the two possible deletion orders have opposite signs, since $(-1)^i(-1)^{j-1}+(-1)^j(-1)^i=0$ for $i<j$. Thus every edge coefficient in the boundary-of-boundary is zero, so the cell row of $DC$ vanishes. This is the transpose of $\partial_2\partial_3=0$.

Periodic identification identifies faces with the prescribed orientation, so the quotient cell structure retains oriented boundary-of-boundary cancellation. For PEC, let $\bar G,\bar C,\bar D$ be the absolute incidence matrices and let $P_e$ select interior edges and $P_v$ select interior vertices. The matrices are $G=P_e\bar G P_v$, $C=\bar C P_e^T$, and $D=\bar D$. An interior vertex is incident to no boundary edge, so $P_e^TP_e\bar G P_v=\bar G P_v$. Hence $CG=\bar C\bar G P_v=0$, while $DC=\bar D\bar C P_e^T=0$. This retains boundary-face magnetic cochains although boundary electric edge values are fixed.

derivations.claim: The matrix $M_e+(\Delta t/2)S$ is symmetric because both summands are symmetric. For each nonzero $x$, its quadratic form is $x^TM_ex+(\Delta t/2)x^TSx>0+0=0$, using $\Delta t>0$ and the two definiteness hypotheses. Hence it is positive definite.

   $$b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}-\Delta t\,C e^n.$$

2. Solve the electric row
   $$\left(M_e+\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^{n+1}=\left(M_e-\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^n+\Delta t\,C^TM_b b^{n+1/2}-\Delta t\,j^{n+1/2}.$$

The row is well defined for every input because its matrix is invertible by [[lem-maxwell-yee-step-matrix-is-positive-definite]]. This procedure makes no stability claim; the lossless stability condition is proved separately.

For the incidence matrices $G,C,D$ of [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], one has $CG=0$ and $DC=0$. The conclusion holds for the full periodic complex and for the PEC mixed closure defined there.

An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. Write $N_v,N_e,N_f,N_c$ for the retained vertex, edge, face, and cell counts. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

The electric, magnetic, and conductive material matrices are real symmetric matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, $M_b\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_f}$, and $S\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, respectively. The first two are positive definite and represent the discrete weighted inner products induced by $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$; $S$ is positive semidefinite and represents conductivity. Write $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle_{M_e}=e_1^TM_ee_2$, $\langle b_1,b_2\rangle_{M_b}=b_1^TM_bb_2$, and $\|e\|_{M_e}^2=\langle e,e\rangle_{M_e}$, $\|b\|_{M_b}^2=\langle b,b\rangle_{M_b}$. These values are dual-volume Hodge weights for line-integral and face-flux cochains. A compatible PEC closure uses the corresponding truncated dual volumes for free electric edges, while the magnetic mass includes boundary faces; the resulting matrices remain positive definite. The discrete constraints are $G^TM_ee^n=\rho^n$ on interior vertices and $Db^{n-1/2}=0$ on all cells.

$$\rho^{n+1}-\rho^n+\Delta t\,G^T\left(j^{n+1/2}+S\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)=0.$$

derivations.claim: If $N_e=0$, the electric cochain is necessarily zero and $C$ is the zero map from the zero space. The Faraday row in [F2] makes $b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}$ at every step, while the electric row is an equality in the zero space. Thus $b_c^n=b^{n+1/2}$ is constant and $\mathcal E^n=\tfrac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2$. With the stated convention $\lambda_{\max}=0$, this proves conservation, the lower bound, and positivity on the remaining magnetic state for every $\Delta t>0$; there is no positive-eigenvalue endpoint case. For the rest of the proof assume $N_e>0$. The quotient defining $\lambda_{\max}$ is continuous on the compact set $\{e:e^TM_ee=1\}$, so the maximum exists and is finite. Also $e^TKe=(Ce)^TM_b(Ce)\ge0$, hence $\lambda_{\max}\ge0$. From the first row of [F2], $b^{n-1/2}=b_c^n+\Delta t Ce^n/2$ and $b^{n+1/2}=b_c^n-\Delta t Ce^n/2$. Expanding their $M_b$ inner product gives $\mathcal E^n=\frac12\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2-\frac{\Delta t^2}{8}\|Ce^n\|_{M_b}^2.$

Using [F2], the electric-energy increment is $\frac12\|e^{n+1}\|_{M_e}^2-\frac12\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2=\left(\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)^TM_e(e^{n+1}-e^n)=\Delta t\left(\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)^TC^TM_bb^{n+1/2}.$ The magnetic cross-energy increment is $\frac12(b^{n+1/2})^TM_b(b^{n+3/2}-b^{n-1/2})=-\Delta t\left(\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)^TC^TM_bb^{n+1/2},$ by applying the Faraday row at times $n$ and $n+1$. The two increments cancel, proving conservation.

By the definition of $\lambda_{\max}$, $\|Ce^n\|_{M_b}^2=(e^n)^TKe^n\le\lambda_{\max}\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2$. Substitution into step 1.1 gives the stated lower bound. When $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}<4$, its electric coefficient is positive. If an admissible staggered state has zero energy, the bound forces $e^n=0$ and $b_c^n=0$; the Faraday row in [F2] then gives $b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}$, so $b_c^n=b^{n-1/2}=b^{n+1/2}=0$. Thus the energy is positive definite on update states.

Subtract the electric row in [F2] at indices $n$ and $n-1$, then use the magnetic row to replace $b^{n+1/2}-b^{n-1/2}$; this gives $M_e(e^{n+1}-2e^n+e^{n-1})+\Delta t^2Ke^n=0$. If $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}=4$, a maximizing vector $v$ satisfies $Kv=\lambda_{\max}M_ev$ by the constrained Rayleigh-quotient maximum. Thus $e^n=q_nv$ obeys $q_{n+1}-2q_n+q_{n-1}+\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}q_n=0$, whose characteristic polynomial is $(r+1)^2$. Hence $q_n=(-1)^n(a+bn)$ is a solution and grows linearly when $b\ne0$. derivations.claim: On a periodic Fourier mode, a forward edge difference in direction $j$ has multiplier $e^{i\theta_j}-1=2i e^{i\theta_j/2}\sin(\theta_j/2)$. The half-cell phase in the edge and face cochain locations is removed by a unitary diagonal change of Fourier basis, so the scaled directional symbol is $i d_j$ with $d_j=2\sin(\theta_j/2)/h_j$. The Cartesian curl symbol is therefore $i\boldsymbol d\times$.

The cross-product matrix $\boldsymbol d\times$ is real skew-symmetric. The identity $-(\boldsymbol d\times)^2=|\boldsymbol d|^2I-\boldsymbol d\boldsymbol d^T$ follows by expanding the vector triple product. Thus the curl-curl symbol is zero on the longitudinal vector $\boldsymbol d$ and equals $|\boldsymbol d|^2$ on its two-dimensional orthogonal complement. The Hodge weights in [F1] scale this eigenvalue by $c^2$, giving the stated $\lambda(\theta)$.

For a transverse mode $e^n=q^n v$ with this eigenvalue, subtracting the electric row in [F3] at consecutive time indices and using its magnetic row gives $q^{n+1}-2q^n+q^{n-1}+\Delta t^2\lambda(\theta)q^n=0$. Substitution of $q^n=e^{-i\omega n\Delta t}$ yields $4\sin^2(\omega\Delta t/2)=\Delta t^2\lambda(\theta)$, which is the displayed dispersion relation.

Since $0\le\sin^2(\theta_j/2)\le1$, $\lambda(\theta)\le4c^2(h_x^{-2}+h_y^{-2}+h_z^{-2})$. When every $N_j$ is even, the allowed tuple $\theta=(\pi,\pi,\pi)$ attains equality; otherwise the exact maximum is the maximum over the finite allowed tuples. Applying [F2] gives the rectangular strict bound and its cubic specialization, while preserving the finite-grid endpoint distinction.

Choose a finite complex and boundary closure as in [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], step size $\Delta t>0$, initial $e^0\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$ and $b^{-1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_f}$, and source rows $j^{n+1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$. The output is a sequence $e^n$ at integer times and $b^{n+1/2}$ at half-integer times. For each $n\ge0$, perform the ordered instructions

1. Update the face flux by
   $$b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}-\Delta t\,C e^n.$$

2. Solve the electric row
   $$\left(M_e+\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^{n+1}=\left(M_e-\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^n+\Delta t\,C^TM_b b^{n+1/2}-\Delta t\,j^{n+1/2}.$$

For $S=0$ this is the lossless Yee leapfrog scheme. For $S\succeq0$, the midpoint term is the specified trapezoidal treatment of conductivity. The row is well defined for every input because its matrix is invertible by [[lem-maxwell-yee-step-matrix-is-positive-definite]]. This procedure makes no stability claim; the lossless stability condition is proved separately.

Let $K$ be a finite oriented three-dimensional cell complex with vertex, edge, face, and volume cochains. An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. Write $N_v,N_e,N_f,N_c$ for the retained vertex, edge, face, and cell counts. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

The electric, magnetic, and conductive material matrices are real symmetric matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, $M_b\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_f}$, and $S\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, respectively. The first two are positive definite and represent the discrete weighted inner products induced by $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$; $S$ is positive semidefinite and represents conductivity. Write $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle_{M_e}=e_1^TM_ee_2$, $\langle b_1,b_2\rangle_{M_b}=b_1^TM_bb_2$, and $\|e\|_{M_e}^2=\langle e,e\rangle_{M_e}$, $\|b\|_{M_b}^2=\langle b,b\rangle_{M_b}$. These values are dual-volume Hodge weights for line-integral and face-flux cochains. A compatible PEC closure uses the corresponding truncated dual volumes for free electric edges, while the magnetic mass includes boundary faces; the resulting matrices remain positive definite. The discrete constraints are $G^TM_ee^n=\rho^n$ on interior vertices and $Db^{n-1/2}=0$ on all cells.

For current cochains $j^{n+1/2}$ and charge rows $\rho^n$, the discrete continuity condition means
$$\rho^{n+1}-\rho^n+\Delta t\,G^T\left(j^{n+1/2}+S\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)=0.$$
For PEC this is the interior-vertex volume-charge relation; this closure has no separate boundary surface-charge/current cochain.

The cochain identities $CG=0$ and $DC=0$ are not imposed as an extra numerical approximation: they follow from oriented boundary-of-boundary cancellation, including the PEC row and column restrictions, as proved in [[lem-maxwell-discrete-incidence-identities]]. Set $K=C^TM_bC$. If the retained electric cochain space is zero-dimensional,
define $\lambda_{\max}:=0$; otherwise set
$$\lambda_{\max}:=\max_{e\ne0}\frac{e^TKe}{e^TM_ee}.$$
For a lossless, source-free update from [[alg-maxwell-yee-leapfrog-update]], define
$$\mathcal E^n:=\frac12(e^n)^TM_ee^n+\frac12(b^{n-1/2})^TM_bb^{n+1/2},\qquad b_c^n:=\frac{b^{n-1/2}+b^{n+1/2}}2.$$
Then $\mathcal E^n$ is independent of $n$, and
$$\mathcal E^n\ge\frac12\left(1-\frac{\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}}4\right)\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2.$$
Consequently, the actual strict spectral condition $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}<4$ makes this modified energy positive on admissible staggered states and controls the electric field and the centered magnetic field. > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The electric trial field is $E_h(t)\in N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$; the magnetic flux field is $B_h(t)\in N_h^2$, with no imposed zero normal trace on $B_h$. PEC means the closure-defined zero tangential subspace from [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Periodic analogues use the periodic cell complex. Countable Choice is inherited from the H(div) and affine Piola space definitions in the suppliers; the finite matrix operations below use no additional choice.

Put $V_h:=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$. Choose an edge basis $\{\phi_i\}_{i=1}^{N_e}$ of the electric trial space $V_h$ and a face basis $\{\psi_a\}_{a=1}^{N_f}$ of $N_h^2$, so $N_e=\dim V_h$ and $N_f=\dim N_h^2$. Define the symmetric mass matrices
$$ (M_e)_{ij}=\int_\Omega \phi_j^T\epsilon\phi_i\,dx,\qquad (M_b)_{ab}=\int_\Omega \psi_b^T\mu^{-1}\psi_a\,dx.$$

The moment-commuting supplier gives $DC=0$ on the full spaces, hence also after restriction to $V_h$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

On an oriented tetrahedron $K$ with vertices $x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3$, let $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ for $0\le i<j\le3$. Then the six edge circulations $\ell_{rs}(v)=\int_{[x_r,x_s]}v\cdot t_{rs}\,ds$ satisfy $\ell_{rs}(\phi_{ij})=\delta_{(r,s),(i,j)}$. The six functions form a basis of the local space $\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:i<j\}=\{a+b\times x:a,b\in\mathbb R^3\}$, so these edge circulations are unisolvent degrees of freedom.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{
abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d=2$ or $3$ and let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ map a reference
simplex to an affine cell with $\det A>0$. The contravariant Piola map
$\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v=(\det A)^{-1}A\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$
maps $H(\operatorname{div},\widehat S_d)$ into $H(\operatorname{div},K)$ and
$$\operatorname{div}(\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v) =(\det A)^{-1}(\widehat{\operatorname{div}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}.$$
The covariant Piola map
$\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}\widehat v=A^{-T}\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$
maps $H(\operatorname{curl},\widehat S_d)$ into $H(\operatorname{curl},K)$;
in $d=2$ its scalar curl is
$(\det A)^{-1}(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$,
and in $d=3$ its vector curl is
$(\det A)^{-1}A(\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}$.
For every $\widehat u\in W^{1,2}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$, the scalar
pullback $u=\widehat u\circ F^{-1}$ belongs to $W^{1,2}(K;\mathbb R)$ and
its gradient satisfies
$$\nabla u=\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}(\widehat\nabla\widehat u).$$
For smooth fields, contravariant normal fluxes satisfy
$v\cdot n\,dS=\widehat v\cdot\widehat n\,d\widehat S$; covariant tangential
pullbacks satisfy $v(F(\widehat x))\cdot A\widehat\tau=
\widehat v(\widehat x)\cdot\widehat\tau$ for every reference tangent
$\widehat\tau$. Thus edge line integrals and normal-flux moments are
preserved, and face tangential moments transform with this pullback and
the induced facet surface Jacobian. These formulas record the chosen
orientation; reversing a facet orientation reverses its signed moment.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

$$\partial_t(\epsilon E)=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)-J_{\rm src}-\sigma E,\qquad \partial_t B+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$
Here $J_{\rm src}$ is the impressed free-current density, while $\sigma E$ is the conductive current. Electric charge $\rho$ is constrained by $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)=\rho$ and the total-current continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E)=0$; the magnetic constraint is $\operatorname{div}B=0$. These equalities are distributional. In the lossless branch set $\sigma=0$.

The boundary choice is one of the following. A **periodic boundary** identifies opposite traces of the rectangular cell. A **perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary** imposes zero tangential trace $n\times E=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. At a material interface with no singular surface charge or current, the weak equations are understood with the transmission conditions $[n\times E]=0$, $[n\cdot B]=0$, $[n\times(\mu^{-1}B)]=0$, and $[n\cdot(\epsilon E)]=0$, where $[q]$ is the trace from one side minus the trace from the other. The interface conditions are part of the model convention; no smooth Taylor expansion across a coefficient jump is asserted.

For PEC, the weak Ampere equation is $(\epsilon E_t,v)_{L^2}-(\mu^{-1}B,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}=-(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ as defined in [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]; the periodic branch uses periodic $H(\operatorname{curl})$ test fields. Faraday’s equation remains $B_t+\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in distributions. These weak forms define the test-space and boundary convention used by the edge finite element method.

The weighted field norms are $\|E\|_\epsilon^2=\int_\Omega E^T\epsilon E\,dx$ and $\|B\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2=\int_\Omega B^T\mu^{-1}B\,dx$. The uniform coefficient bounds make them equivalent to the ordinary $L^2$ norms. All later smooth-error claims require smoothness separately on each mesh-aligned material region.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Use the preceding mesh-size and boundary-shift lemma. All differential-form notation here is the following finite coefficient notation. A degree-$k$ form in $\mathbb R^3$ is $u=\sum_{I}u_I\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, where the sum is over increasing $k$-tuples $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$, the wedge is alternating, and $\|u\|_2^2=\sum_I\|u_I\|_2^2$. The empty wedge is one. Put $du=\sum_I\sum_{j=1}^3(\partial_j u_I)dx^j\wedge dx^I$, with derivatives interpreted distributionally through integration by parts against compactly supported scalar tests; repeated differentials are zero. The graph space $H\Lambda^k$ consists of the coefficient vectors with $u,du\in L^2$, with norm squared $\|u\|_2^2+\|du\|_2^2$; in top degree $d=0$. These formulas agree with the proved smooth coordinate exterior derivative. Identify vector fields with forms by $\sum_{i=1}^3u_i dx_i$ in degree one, $v_1dx_2\wedge dx_3+v_2dx_3\wedge dx_1+v_3dx_1\wedge dx_2$ in degree two, and $q\,dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3$ in degree three. Thus expansion of the finite formula for $d$ gives grad, curl, and div with exactly these signs; the degree-two coefficients in increasing order are $(v_3,-v_2,v_1)$, so their Euclidean norm equals that of $v$. For a smooth map $G$ from an open subset of $\mathbb R^q$ to $\mathbb R^3$, define its pullback by the finite tangent-Jacobian-minor formula
$$G^*u=\sum_{J}\left(\sum_I u_I(G)\det\bigl(\partial_{j_b}G^{i_a}\bigr)_{a,b=1}^k\right)\,dt^{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dt^{j_k}.$$
Here $J$ ranges over increasing $k$-tuples in $1,\ldots,q$; in degree zero this is composition. If $a:T_k\to\sigma$ is the oriented affine simplex parametrization, define $\int_\sigma G^*u$ as the integral over $T_k$ of the coefficient of $(G\circ a)^*u$ on its positive top wedge. Orientation reversal changes its sign; in degree zero it is evaluation. For averaged moments of merely $L^2$ coefficients, the joint parameter integral is the definition and the estimates below prove it exists and is representative-independent. No unbounded trace of an $L^2$ form on a fixed lower-dimensional surface is being defined. This is the existing smooth simplex-integration convention, extended only through the displayed integrable averages. Write $E_h^k$ for the four full Whitney spaces and $E_{h,0}^k$ for the subspaces with all boundary $k$-simplex moments zero; $E_{h,0}^3=E_h^3$. Let $H_0\Lambda^k$ be the graph closure of compactly supported smooth $k$-forms; in degrees zero and one these are $H_0^1$ and the defined $H_0(\operatorname{curl})$.

Fix nonnegative $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B_1)$ with integral one. For each oriented mesh $k$-simplex $\sigma$, define
$$m_{\sigma}^{+,k}(u)=\int_{B_1}\rho(y)\int_\sigma(F_{\epsilon,y}^{+})^*u\,dy,\qquad m_{\sigma}^{-,k}(u)=\int_{B_1}\rho(y)\int_\sigma(F_{\epsilon,y}^{-})^*\widetilde u\,dy,$$
where $\widetilde u$ is zero extension and a degree-zero simplex integral is evaluation. Whitney reconstruction from these moments defines $Q_h^{+,k}:L^2\Lambda^k\to E_h^k$ and $Q_h^{-,k}:L^2\Lambda^k\to E_{h,0}^k$. For $0<\epsilon\le\epsilon_0$,
$$\|Q_h^{\pm,k}u\|_2\le C\epsilon^{-3/2}\|u\|_2,\qquad \|(Q_h^{\pm,k}-I)v_h\|_2\le C\epsilon\|v_h\|_2,$$
where the second bound uses respectively $v_h\in E_h^k$ or $v_h\in E_{h,0}^k$. Constants are independent of $h,\epsilon$. For $k=0,1,2$, $dQ_h^{+,k}=Q_h^{+,k+1}d$ on $H\Lambda^k$ and $dQ_h^{-,k}=Q_h^{-,k+1}d$ on $H_0\Lambda^k$. In degree three, both exterior derivatives are zero. The relative Whitney spaces equal $E_h^k\cap H_0\Lambda^k$.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{
abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open and set
$$H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)}^{\,H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)},$$
where the norm is that of [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. This is the closure-defined zero-tangential subspace used on this page. Identifying this closure with the full kernel of a particular boundary trace map is not part of the definition.

derivations.claim: We first justify the closure and time derivatives; $E_t,E_{tt}$ denote the classical time derivatives. For each $u=E(t),E_t(t),E_{tt}(t)$, zero boundary tangential trace makes the boundary edge moments of $I_h^1u$ zero, so [F7] gives $I_h^1u\in V_h$. By [F4], $I_h^1u\to u$ in $H(\operatorname{curl})$ as $h\to0$, and [F9] gives $u\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$. Uniform bounds on $E_{tt}$ give $L^2$-Lipschitz continuity of $E_t$ by the pointwise mean-value bound [F8]. For a compact smooth vector test $\psi$, dominated differentiation gives $\frac d{dt}(\operatorname{curl}E_t,\psi)=\frac d{dt}(E_t,\operatorname{curl}\psi)=(E_{tt},\operatorname{curl}\psi)=(\operatorname{curl}E_{tt},\psi)$. The uniform bound on $\operatorname{curl}E_{tt}$ and [F8], followed by $L^2$ density, therefore give $\|\operatorname{curl}E_t(t)-\operatorname{curl}E_t(s)\|_2\le K|t-s|$. The same test identities for $E$ show $E$ is graph-norm $C^1$ with derivative $E_t$: subtract the value of $E_t(s)$ from its difference quotient and use the just-proved Lipschitz bound, first in test pairings and then by density. Difference quotients of $E_t$ are uniformly graph bounded; their $L^2$ parts converge to $E_{tt}$ by dominated convergence, and their curls converge distributionally to $\operatorname{curl}E_{tt}$. Density and uniform boundedness upgrade the latter to weak $L^2$ convergence. Consequently every bounded graph-linear functional of $E_t$ is differentiable with derivative its value on $E_{tt}$. In particular the finite Ritz Gram equations give $(R_hE)_t=R_hE_t$ and $(R_hE)_{tt}=R_hE_{tt}$, with a bounded second derivative; continuity of $E_{tt}$ in the graph norm is unnecessary.

The initialization gives $\theta_h(0)=0$. Test the semidiscrete Ampere row at $t=0$ and subtract the exact weak row. By the curl orthogonality in [F5], $(\mu^{-1}(B_h^0-B(0)),\operatorname{curl}v_h)=0$ for every $v_h$, so $\dot E_h(0)$ is the $\epsilon$-orthogonal projection of $E_t(0)$ onto $V_h$. The zero tangential boundary trace gives zero boundary edge moments for $I_h^1E_t(0)$; [F7] therefore places this interpolant in $V_h$. Its best-approximation error is at most $\|E_t(0)-I_h^1E_t(0)\|_\epsilon\le Ch$ by [F4]. Also $\|R_hE_t(0)-E_t(0)\|_\epsilon\le Ch$ by [F3,F4]. Hence $\|\dot\theta_h(0)\|_\epsilon\le Ch$.

Differentiate the exact weak Ampere equation in [F2] and use $B_t=-\operatorname{curl}E$. Since $\mu$ is time-independent, this gives, for every $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$, $(\epsilon E_{tt},v)+(\mu^{-1}\operatorname{curl}E,\operatorname{curl}v)=-(\partial_tJ_{\rm src},v).$ Differentiating the finite-dimensional Ampere row and using $\dot b+Ce=0$ gives the identical Galerkin equation for $E_h$: $(\epsilon \ddot E_h,v_h)+(\mu^{-1}\operatorname{curl}E_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)=-(\partial_tJ_{\rm src},v_h).$ The solution exists by [F1]; the exact time pairings are differentiable by step 1.1, and the discrete differentiation is valid because $J_{\rm src}$ is $C^1$.

Let $R_h$ be fixed in time and put $\theta_h=E_h-R_hE$. Step 1.1 justifies $(R_hE)_{tt}=R_hE_{tt}$ for its time-independent Gram matrix. Subtract the two equations in step 2.1 and use Ritz orthogonality [F3], namely $a(E-R_hE,v_h)=-m(E-R_hE,v_h)$. For every $v_h\in V_h$ this yields $m(\ddot\theta_h,v_h)+a(\theta_h,v_h)=m((I-R_h)(E_{tt}-E),v_h).$ The zero tangential boundary trace gives zero boundary edge moments for $I_h^1(E_{tt}-E)$, so [F7] places this interpolant in $V_h$. Best approximation [F3] and the canonical estimate [F4] then show uniformly in time that $\|(I-R_h)(E_{tt}-E)\|_\epsilon\le C h$.

Define $Q_h(t)=\tfrac12(\|\dot\theta_h(t)\|_\epsilon^2+\|\operatorname{curl}\theta_h(t)\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2)$. Test the equation in step 3.1 with $v_h=\dot\theta_h$. Symmetry gives $Q_h'(t)=m((I-R_h)(E_{tt}-E),\dot\theta_h),\qquad |Q_h'(t)|\le\|(I-R_h)(E_{tt}-E)\|_\epsilon\sqrt{2Q_h(t)}.$ For $\delta>0$, the derivative of $\sqrt{Q_h+\delta}$ has absolute value at most $Ch/\sqrt2$ by step 3.1. The scalar mean-value bound [F8], the initial estimate in step 1.2 and then $\delta\downarrow0$ give $\sqrt{Q_h(t)}\le Ch$ on $[0,T]$. The finite-dimensional mean-value bound and $\theta_h(0)=0$ also give $\sup_t\|\theta_h(t)\|_\epsilon\le T\sup_t\|\dot\theta_h(t)\|_\epsilon\le Ch$.

By step 4.1, $\theta_h$ is $O(h)$ in the electric $L^2$ norm and its curl norm. The Ritz best-approximation estimate [F3] and interpolation estimate [F4] give $\|R_hE-E\|_{L^2}+\|\operatorname{curl}(R_hE-E)\|_{L^2}\le Ch$. The triangle inequality therefore gives the asserted electric and curl error bound.

Subtract the exact Faraday equation from the semidiscrete magnetic row and integrate in time: $B_h(t)-B(t)=B_h^0-B(0)-\int_0^t\operatorname{curl}(E_h(s)-E(s))\,ds.$ The initial difference is $O(h)$ by [F5], and the curl error is $O(h)$ uniformly by step 5.1, so the magnetic $L^2$ error is at most $Ch+TCh$. Also $D B_h(t)=D B_h^0-\int_0^t D C e_h(s)\,ds=0$ by [F5] and the discrete identity $DC=0$ in [F2]. Norm equivalence [F6] completes the result.

Consider a homogeneous isotropic periodic Yee grid with $\epsilon,\mu>0$, wave speed $c=(\epsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$, spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$, and $N_x,N_y,N_z$ cells. Its allowed wave angles are $\theta_j=2\pi m_j/N_j$. On a mode with wave vector $k_j=\theta_j/h_j$, the transverse curl-curl eigenvalue is
$$\lambda(\theta)=c^2\sum_{j\in\{x,y,z\}}\frac{4}{h_j^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta_j}{2}\right),$$
and the lossless Yee leapfrog dispersion relation is
$$\sin^2\left(\frac{\omega\Delta t}{2}\right)=c^2\Delta t^2\sum_{j\in\{x,y,z\}}\frac{\sin^2(\theta_j/2)}{h_j^2}.$$
The exact finite-grid strict condition is $\Delta t^2\max_{\theta}\lambda(\theta)<4$, as in [[thm-maxwell-yee-strict-cfl-modified-energy]]. The rectangular sufficient bound is
$$\Delta t<\frac{1}{c\sqrt{h_x^{-2}+h_y^{-2}+h_z^{-2}}};$$
it is exact when every $N_j$ is even. For a cubic grid this bound is $\Delta t<h/(c\sqrt3)$. Odd cell counts may have a smaller finite-grid maximum, so the finite-grid eigenvalue is the exact criterion.

derivations.claim: For $\theta=(\pi,0,0)$, the sine-square sum is $1$, so $\sin^2(\omega_{\rm ax}\Delta t/2)=c^2\Delta t^2/h^2$. Its symbol direction is the $x$-axis, and $p=(0,1,0)$ is orthogonal to it, so this is a transverse mode.

For $\theta=(\pi,\pi,\pi)$, the sum is $3$ and $p=(1,-1,0)/\sqrt2$ is orthogonal to $(1,1,1)$. Thus $\sin^2(\omega_{\rm corner}\Delta t/2)=3c^2\Delta t^2/h^2$. The maximum eigenvalue is $12c^2/h^2$, so strict positivity requires $\Delta t<h/(c\sqrt3)$; equality places the maximal mode at the repeated-root endpoint.

Choose a finite complex and boundary closure as in [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], step size $\Delta t>0$, initial $e^0\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$ and $b^{-1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_f}$, and source rows $j^{n+1/2}\in\mathbb R^{N_e}$. The output is a sequence $e^n$ at integer times and $b^{n+1/2}$ at half-integer times. For each $n\ge0$, perform the ordered instructions

1. Update the face flux by
   $$b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}-\Delta t\,C e^n.$$

2. Solve the electric row
   $$\left(M_e+\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^{n+1}=\left(M_e-\frac{\Delta t}{2}S\right)e^n+\Delta t\,C^TM_b b^{n+1/2}-\Delta t\,j^{n+1/2}.$$

For $S=0$ this is the lossless Yee leapfrog scheme. For $S\succeq0$, the midpoint term is the specified trapezoidal treatment of conductivity. The row is well defined for every input because its matrix is invertible by [[lem-maxwell-yee-step-matrix-is-positive-definite]]. This procedure makes no stability claim; the lossless stability condition is proved separately.

For the incidence matrices $G,C,D$ of [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], one has $CG=0$ and $DC=0$. The conclusion holds for the full periodic complex and for the PEC mixed closure defined there.

Let $K$ be a finite oriented three-dimensional cell complex with vertex, edge, face, and volume cochains. An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. Write $N_v,N_e,N_f,N_c$ for the retained vertex, edge, face, and cell counts. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

The electric, magnetic, and conductive material matrices are real symmetric matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, $M_b\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_f}$, and $S\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_e}$, respectively. The first two are positive definite and represent the discrete weighted inner products induced by $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$; $S$ is positive semidefinite and represents conductivity. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lipschitz polyhedron, or a periodic rectangular cell. The real electric field is $E(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$ and the magnetic flux density is $B(t,x)\in\mathbb R^3$; the magnetic intensity is $H=\mu^{-1}B$. Let $\epsilon(x)$ and $\mu(x)$ be measurable, time-independent, symmetric matrix fields for which there are constants $0<\epsilon_0\le\epsilon_1$ and $0<\mu_0\le\mu_1$ with
$$\epsilon_0|v|^2\le v^T\epsilon(x)v\le\epsilon_1|v|^2,\qquad \mu_0|v|^2\le v^T\mu(x)v\le\mu_1|v|^2$$
for almost every $x$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. A conductivity tensor $\sigma(x)$, when present, is measurable, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The coefficients may jump across finitely many Lipschitz material interfaces. No derivative of a coefficient is part of the model.

In each material region the constitutive fields satisfy
$$\partial_t(\epsilon E)=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)-J_{\rm src}-\sigma E,\qquad \partial_t B+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$
Here $J_{\rm src}$ is the impressed free-current density, while $\sigma E$ is the conductive current. Electric charge $\rho$ is constrained by $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)=\rho$ and the total-current continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E)=0$; the magnetic constraint is $\operatorname{div}B=0$. These equalities are distributional. In the lossless branch set $\sigma=0$.

The boundary choice is one of the following. A **periodic boundary** identifies opposite traces of the rectangular cell. A **perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary** imposes zero tangential trace $n\times E=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. At a material interface with no singular surface charge or current, the weak equations are understood with the transmission conditions $[n\times E]=0$, $[n\cdot B]=0$, $[n\times(\mu^{-1}B)]=0$, and $[n\cdot(\epsilon E)]=0$, where $[q]$ is the trace from one side minus the trace from the other. The interface conditions are part of the model convention; no smooth Taylor expansion across a coefficient jump is asserted.

For PEC, the weak Ampere equation is $(\epsilon E_t,v)_{L^2}-(\mu^{-1}B,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}=-(J_{\rm src}+\sigma E,v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ as defined in [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]; the periodic branch uses periodic $H(\operatorname{curl})$ test fields. Faraday’s equation remains $B_t+\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in distributions. These weak forms define the test-space and boundary convention used by the edge finite element method.

The weighted field norms are $\|E\|_\epsilon^2=\int_\Omega E^T\epsilon E\,dx$ and $\|B\|_{\mu^{-1}}^2=\int_\Omega B^T\mu^{-1}B\,dx$. The uniform coefficient bounds make them equivalent to the ordinary $L^2$ norms. All later smooth-error claims require smoothness separately on each mesh-aligned material region.

derivations.claim: The tangential electric field vanishes on $x=0,a$ and $y=0,b$ because $\Phi=0$ there; it also vanishes on $z=0,d$ because the only component of $E$ is normal to those faces. Direct differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{div}(\epsilon E)=0$. Thus both divergence constraints and the PEC trace hold.

Differentiation gives $B_t=-\operatorname{curl}E$. The $z$ component of $\operatorname{curl}B$ is $-(k_x^2+k_y^2)\Phi\sin(\omega t)/\omega$, with the other two components zero. Since $\epsilon\omega^2=(k_x^2+k_y^2)/\mu$, the expression $-(k_x^2+k_y^2)\Phi\sin(\omega t)/(\mu\omega)$ equals $-\epsilon\omega\Phi\sin(\omega t)=\epsilon E_t$. Hence $\epsilon E_t=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)$. The angular frequency is therefore $\omega=(\epsilon\mu)^{-1/2}\sqrt{(m\pi/a)^2+(n\pi/b)^2}$.
